newsitem.title: NORWAY: Strong Norway economy risks overheating - OECD.
newsitem.headline: Strong Norway economy risks overheating - OECD.

text.p: The booming Norwegian economy is operating near capacity and could start overheating unless a restrictive monetary policy is pursued, the Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) said on Tuesday.
It noted in a survey that Norway's oil-driven economy had expanded rapidly with overall real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth averaging 4.5 percent in the past three years.
Excluding petroleum production, mainland GDP growth averaged almmost 3.5 percent, creating more jobs and reducing the jobless rate to a seasonally adjusted 4.5 percent by the end of 1996.
It said the developments suggested "that the economy is now operating close to capacity".
Labour reserves may soon be exhausted, which would create upward pressure on wages and help fuel inflation, it said.

The current macro-economic policy framework -- with monetary policy focussing on exchange rate stability against European currencies -- is coming under strain now that the risk of inflationary tensions is rising, the survey said.
"Consequently, a restrictive monetary policy is now necessary," it said.

OECD noted that the central bank deposit rates, which constitute the floor for money market rates, had been cut by some 150 basis points since March 1996 in attempts to keep the currency from appreciating too much.

"These developments have contributed to higher asset prices, both in the real estate and stock markets. With, as noted, the economy running near potential, such a course, if maintained, risks providing undue impetus to domestic credit and private demand, with resultant overheating.

"Therefore, whatever room exists for tightening monetary conditions, within the present framework of maintaining a stable exchange rate over the medium term, needs to be used to forestall an acceleration of inflation," OECD said.
In a short-term outlook, the survey projected overall GDP growth would slow down from five percent in 1996 to three percent this year and 2.3 percent next year.
This forecast was based on an expected levelling off in petroleum production and a moderation of domestic demand.

With economic activity in Europe picking up, demand for traditional exports should remain fairly strong. Accordingly, the mainland economy was projected to expand by 2.5 percent in 1997 and by 2.1 percent in 1998.

With labour market conditions tightening, wage growth was projected to accelerate to over five percent and inflation, a modest 1.25 percent in 1996, could creep up to around 2.5 percent this year and broadly remain at that level in 1998.
Despite an anticipated correction of the oil price hike, the current account surplus is expected to remain above six percent of GDP, OECD said.
